title: SEBI Defends India's New Closing Auction as Market Volatility Concerns Persist
excerpt: India's securities regulator has ruled out an immediate review of the new closing auction session despite sharp price swings and thin liquidity in its first two weeks of operation.
body:
• SEBI chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said no manipulation has been detected in the new Closing Auction Session, calling it a "big market structure reform" in line with global standards.
  • Mutual fund participation has risen from 5–6% on the first day to about 20–25%, but arbitrage funds worth ₹3.4 trillion remain largely absent from the new mechanism.
  • BSE's auction value of just ₹9.4 crore versus NSE's ₹1,542.4 crore highlights a sharp liquidity imbalance between the two exchanges.
  • SEBI has asked brokers to display indicative equilibrium prices on trading platforms and educate retail investors on the auction process.

India's markets regulator has ruled out an immediate review of the newly introduced Closing Auction Session (CAS) despite persistent concerns about price volatility, thin liquidity and sharp divergences between the Nifty and Sensex in the mechanism's first two weeks.

Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Wednesday that no manipulation had been observed so far, describing the auction as a major structural reform aligned with global best practices.

"We are considering all inputs to increase participation," Pandey said at an event in Mumbai, adding that any new system requires time to settle.

What Changed and Why

The CAS replaced the previous method of calculating closing prices using the volume-weighted average price (VWAP) of trades in the final 30 minutes of continuous trading. Under the new framework, which went live on August 3 for stocks in the futures and options segment, continuous trading ends at 3:15 p.m., followed by a 20-minute auction session running until 3:35 p.m.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=sY3ul8h70mY

During the auction window, exchanges collect buy and sell orders and match them at a single equilibrium price that maximizes executed volume. The reform was designed to provide a fairer and more transparent closing price, reduce tracking error for passive funds and improve execution efficiency for large institutional orders, according to Reuters.

Rocky Start

The debut was anything but smooth. On the first day, the Nifty 50 surged nearly 200 points in the final two minutes of the auction, a 1.6% spike that stunned traders. The Sensex, meanwhile, rose just 0.7% — an unusual divergence that persisted across the first week, according to Mint.

On the second trading day, the Nifty fell 0.64% while the Sensex dropped just 0.27%. The gap widened further on options expiry days, when thin liquidity in the BSE auction magnified price swings.

Data from the exchanges showed BSE's auction value at a mere ₹9.4 crore compared with ₹1,542.4 crore on the NSE, underscoring the liquidity imbalance. Many traders reported they could not see indicative auction prices before placing orders, making it difficult to gauge where the market was likely to settle, BusinessLine reported.

Arbitrage Funds on the Sidelines

A key concern is the absence of arbitrage funds, which typically provide crucial liquidity in the final minutes of trading. A fund manager told Mint that roughly ₹3.4 trillion of arbitrage funds managed by mutual fund houses are unlikely to participate in CAS because neither the final execution price nor the allocated quantity is known in advance.

"This meant that supply could not match with demand from other large institutional players, leading to price spikes during the auction."

— A broker present at SEBI's meeting with market intermediaries, as reported by Mint

The structural issue stems from the earlier close of continuous trading at 3:15 p.m. Arbitrage funds need to execute buy and sell legs simultaneously to hedge exposure, which becomes impossible when the cash market closes 25 minutes before derivatives trading ends at 3:40 p.m.

SEBI's Response

Rather than revisiting the framework, SEBI has focused on improving participation and transparency. The regulator met large brokers on multiple occasions during the first week, asking them to visibly display indicative equilibrium prices and educate clients about the auction mechanism.

"The framework was cleared after thorough review. It's too soon to evaluate a review," a person aware of the discussions told BusinessLine.

Mutual fund participation has improved, rising from about 5–6% on the first day to 20–25%, according to the SEBI chairman. But market participants say broader retail and institutional engagement will be critical, particularly on index rebalancing and derivatives expiry days when passive funds execute large portfolio adjustments.

What's Next

The auction's impact on weekly options expiry — particularly for the Sensex on BSE, where liquidity remains razor-thin — will be closely watched in coming weeks. SEBI has indicated it may eventually expand CAS to stocks beyond the current futures and options segment, but only after the initial rollout demonstrates stability.

For now, the regulator is betting that familiarity and improved broker infrastructure will gradually draw more participants into the auction, narrowing the liquidity gaps and price swings that have defined its debut.
